source_read: PMC HTML, PMC6776700: the author manuscript (NIHMS1534273) of Am J Gastroenterol 2019;114(10):1574-1586, not the version of record; page title confirmed in my own tab. Whole text read with get_page_text (56,811 characters, complete, ending at the supplementary-materials note): abstract, introduction, methods, results with Table 1 (rendered as text), discussion, Study Highlights, financial support, declaration of interests and reference list. Figures 1-5 (flow chart and forest plots, images only) read on PMC's figure page, enlarged on screen (study and estimate columns side by side at 1.8x for Figure 2). Supplementary file (.docx: Supplementary Tables 1-2, Supplementary Figures 1-7) not read.

claims.overstatement: Minor: 'general-population cohorts' is generous. The cohorts are American Cancer Society volunteers, registered nurses, Kaiser Permanente members, women attending breast screening, Danish Diet, Cancer and Health participants and a Chinese surveillance-point sample, and the review itself says low response rates and screening-programme inclusion may limit generalisability (Discussion, 5th paragraph). The association wording ('is associated with ... grows with the amount') matches the source. Nothing reads as advice on amounts.
claims.note: Every Roerecke number in the statement and magnitude matches the source: Figure 2 for the six cohort estimates and I2 (70.6% to 98.6%); Figures 2 and 3 for 1.80, 8.30 and 22.39 at 7 or more drinks in the three men's cohorts (Yang, China; Klatsky, Kaiser Permanente; Boffetta, ACS); Figure 5 for the four case-control estimates; 2,629,272 participants and 5,505 cases; one drink = 12 g a day; NIAAA funding. Recomputed: Table 1 reproduces 2,629,272 participants (579,592 men), 5,505 cases (2,196 men and 3,309 women). The 'about 1.24' correction is exp(0.23 x ln 2.52) = 1.237, or 1.241 with the Results' 2.56, so 1.24 either way; it applies to exactly four cohorts whose reference group was current abstainers (Boffetta, Garfinkel, Liu, Yang). The reference groups are named correctly: long-term abstainers for the cohort pool (partly by that correction) and lifetime abstainers for the case-control studies. Three points to consider. (1) The pooled cohort figures combine men's and women's estimates and each rests on few studies: 5, 6, 6, 5, 5 and 4 cohorts (6, 7, 7, 5, 6 and 5 sex-specific estimates) with 458, 1,111, 574, 203, 281 and 276 cases from occasional drinking to 7 or more drinks (editors' sums from Figure 2). The claim gives only the review-wide totals. (2) The Danish cohort is in the review in a different form from the cohort paper. Table 1 lists it with 393 cases in men and 229 in women and outcome codes that include unspecified cirrhosis (K74.6 and others), and only women's rows appear in Figures 2 and 4 (lifetime abstainers given as 0.002% of the men). So 'the Danish cohort counted only cirrhosis recorded as alcoholic' (257 and 85 cases, as quoted from the cohort paper) is true of the cohort paper but not of the data this review pooled. (3) 'Outcome was mostly death from cirrhosis' is fair: the text says all cohorts included cirrhosis mortality, and Table 1 shows hospital or patient-register records added for the Million Women and Danish cohorts. 'The two meta-analyses share six studies' cannot be checked from this source alone.

anchors.extracted: 7 cohort and 2 case-control studies; 2,629,272 participants (579,592 men, 2,049,680 women) and 5,505 cirrhosis cases (2,196 men, 3,309 women); 4 US, 2 Italian, 1 each from China, UK and Denmark. All cohorts included cirrhosis mortality as the outcome (Table 1: Danish and Million Women cohorts also used patient or hospital registers); the 2 case-control studies used first diagnosis of symptomatic cirrhosis against lifetime abstainers. Intake was measured once at baseline in every cohort; the Italian case-control studies recalled lifetime intake. Totals recomputed from Table 1 match.

anchors.extracted: Intake converted to g/day from category midpoints; categories with a mean of up to 12 g of pure ethanol counted as one standard drink; legend: 1 standard drink = 12 g pure ethanol per day. DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooling of the most adjusted RRs; sex-specific estimates treated as independent samples (Data extraction).

Cohorts, RR vs long-term abstainers (95% CI; I2): occasional 1.11 (0.77-1.59; 70.6%); 1 drink/day 1.40 (1.00-1.97; 78.2%); 2 drinks 3.02 (1.95-4.70; 91.7%); 3-4 drinks 3.27 (0.90-11.87; 98.6%); 5-6 drinks 6.26 (2.38-16.50; 96.7%); 7 or more 10.70 (2.95-38.78; 98.3%). 6, 7, 7, 5, 6 and 5 sex-specific estimates from 5, 6, 6, 5, 5 and 4 cohorts; 458, 1,111, 574, 203, 281 and 276 cases (editors' sums). Text gives only the 7-or-more estimate and 'I2 between 70 and 98%'.

Men's cohorts at 7 or more drinks a day: Yang 2012 (Chinese men) 1.80 (1.38-2.36); Klatsky 2003 (Kaiser Permanente, USA) 8.30 (3.97-17.34); Boffetta 1990 (American Cancer Society, USA) 22.39 (17.45-28.72). At 3-4 drinks, single-cohort estimates range from 1.04 (0.87-1.25) to 14.21 (10.77-18.75).

Two Italian hospital case-control studies vs lifetime abstainers: 1-4 drinks/day 1.19 (0.58-2.43; I2 59.7%); 5-8 drinks 3.42 (1.31-8.96; 79.0%); 9-13 drinks 7.36 (1.91-28.34; 86.3%); 13 or more 5.71 (2.87-11.33; 0%, Corrao 1993 only). Corrao 1997 showed large increases in both sexes, Corrao 1993 none or marginal ones.

Results give the pooled former-drinker RR as 2.56 (0.93-6.79) from two cohorts, with 23% former drinkers among current abstainers. Current-abstainer reference in Boffetta, Garfinkel, Liu and Yang (4 cohorts). Editors' calculation: x1.237 (2.52) or x1.241 (2.56).

anchors.extracted: No clear indication of a threshold, rated low quality for imprecision and few sex-specific estimates at low intake; spline tests for non-linearity P = 0.24 (men) and 0.27 (women), with little power. The discussion nevertheless reports some evidence for a threshold effect in men. GRADE for a causal effect: moderate.

anchors.locator: Table 1, Askgaard et al. 2015 row; Results, 1st paragraph; Figures 2 and 4
anchors.extracted: In the review, the Danish cohort has 393 cases in men and 229 in women (26,696 and 29,221 participants; 14.9 years), with outcome codes K70.3 plus unspecified cirrhosis (ICD-10 I85.0, I85.9, K74.6, R18.9) from the patient and death registers. Only women's estimates appear in the forest plots (144, 41 and 38 cases at 1, 3-4 and 5-6 drinks); lifetime abstainers are given as 0.002% of the men.

All cohorts but one rated moderate risk of bias (ROBINS-I), mainly for single baseline intake and observational design; Garfinkel 1988 rated serious (age-only adjustment). Limitations: few studies; single intake measurement (regression dilution); self-report may underestimate intake; low response rates and screening-programme samples may limit generalisability; case-control recall bias.

claims.overstatement: None for this source's part: the claim keeps association wording, whereas the review's Study Highlights say daily drinking and drinking outside meals 'increases' risk at any given intake, from single observational studies.
claims.note: The review's figures are quoted correctly: Danish cohort, daily vs 2-4 days a week, 'adjusted for weekly alcohol intake', men 2.25 (1.68-3.00) and women 1.28 (0.82-2.02); Million Women Study, among drinkers, daily vs non-daily 1.61 (1.40-1.85), with meals vs outside meals 0.69 (0.62-0.77), daily and outside meals together 2.47 (1.96-3.11). One small wording point. The review states 'adjustment for amount and type of beverage' only for the joint 2.47 estimate. For 1.61 and 0.69 it gives no adjustment set; it says only that they were similar across strata of BMI, smoking and beverage type, and the Highlights say 'at any given level of overall alcohol intake'. So 'with amount and beverage taken into account' attached to 1.61 is an inference, not this source's statement. Whether the Danish figures are in the cohort paper's main text cannot be checked from this source.

anchors.extracted: Askgaard 2015 frequency results adjusted for weekly intake: daily vs 2-4 days/week, men RR 2.25 (1.68-3.00), women 1.28 (0.82-2.02). Million Women Study among drinkers: daily vs non-daily 1.61 (1.40-1.85); with meals vs outside meals 0.69 (0.62-0.77); similar across strata of BMI, smoking and beverage type; daily and outside meals 2.47 (1.96-3.11), adjusted for amount and beverage type.

The authors read frequency as modifying risk at a given weekly intake (fewer drinking days, lower risk; 'liver holiday'), cite the Singapore Chinese Health Study (daily drinkers, one drink a day, RR 2.72, 0.98-7.50, vs non-drinkers), and call evidence on binge drinking limited and inconclusive. The Highlights state daily drinking and drinking outside meals increase risk at any given intake.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim is more careful than the source: the abstract says women's risk was 'consistently higher' and the Results say women's RRs were higher at all levels, which the review's own occasional-drinking estimates contradict (0.95 against 1.23).
claims.note: All twelve sex-specific estimates match Figures 3 and 4: occasional 0.95 (0.77-1.16) against 1.23 (0.46-3.28); 1 drink 1.64 (1.07-2.51) against 0.91 (0.31-2.64); 2 drinks 4.33 (2.59-7.25) against 1.97 (0.89-4.37); 3-4 drinks 3.87 (0.80-18.83) against 2.62 (0.42-16.21); 5-6 drinks 12.44 (6.65-23.27) against 3.80 (0.85-17.02); 7 or more 24.58 (14.77-40.90) against 6.93 (1.07-44.99). Women's levels pool 4, 5, 4, 3, 3 and 2 cohorts and men's 2, 2, 3, 2, 3 and 3. Garfinkel 1988 (ACS women, baseline 1959-60, age-standardised only, the one cohort rated serious risk of bias) carries 52.49% and 77.38% of the weight at 5-6 and 7 or more drinks, which gives the claim's 52% and 77%. At 1 drink the two men's cohorts point in opposite directions (Klatsky 0.50, 0.25-1.02; Boffetta 1.50, 1.07-2.10). No test of a sex difference is reported in the main text, and the discussion says the intervals overlapped; in this review they overlap at every level. One qualifier the claim leaves out: the review reports that restricting to the four women's cohorts adjusted for age, BMI or waist and smoking (which leaves out Garfinkel) gave a similar, linearly rising relationship from 1 drink (Results, 3rd paragraph; values only in Supplementary Figure 3, not read). At 5 or more drinks that subset leaves only the Danish and Kaiser Permanente cohorts.

anchors.extracted: Garfinkel 1988 (ACS women recruited 1959-60, age-standardised only, rated serious risk of bias) weights 52.49% at 5-6 drinks and 77.38% at 7 or more. Men's cohorts at 1 drink: Klatsky 0.50 (0.25-1.02), Boffetta 1.50 (1.07-2.10); two or three men's cohorts per level.

The authors say the increase was stronger in women but the intervals were large and overlapped with men's, and urge caution because of few studies; no formal test of a sex difference is given. Sensitivity analysis: four women's cohorts adjusted for age, BMI or waist and smoking showed an elevated, linearly increasing risk from 1 drink (Supplementary Figure 3).

key_findings.correction: The review states the adjustment 'for amount and type of beverage' only for the joint estimate (daily and outside meals, 2.47, 1.96-3.11). For daily vs non-daily (1.61) and with vs outside meals (0.69) it gives no adjustment set; it says only that they were similar across strata of BMI, smoking and beverage type (the Highlights add 'at any given level of overall alcohol intake'). Suggested wording: '... daily and outside meals together 2.47 (1.96-3.11), adjusted for amount and beverage type; the other two estimates are given without a stated adjustment set'. The numbers are right.

Likewise, the text's 'I2 between 70 and 98%' understates Figure 2's maximum of 98.6% (trivial).

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low confidence follows from items 2 (no protocol) and 7 (no list of excluded studies) alone. Item 11 is the debatable one, since the techniques themselves are standard and the 'no' rests on pooling at I2 near 99% and the fixed former-drinker correction; changing it would not change the overall rating. Item 3 'no' is also arguable (restricting to observational designs with an abstainer comparator is self-explanatory), again without effect on the overall rating.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. One more gap: the Study Highlights state as causal ('increases the risk ... at any given level of overall alcohol intake') that daily drinking and drinking outside meals raise risk, from one cohort per pattern.

missed: The Danish cohort enters the review in a different form from the cohort paper: Table 1 gives 393 cases in men and 229 in women with outcome codes that include unspecified cirrhosis (ICD-10 I85.0, I85.9, K74.6, R18.9), and the forest plots carry only its women (144, 41 and 38 cases at 1, 3-4 and 5-6 drinks). The cohort paper's alcoholic-cirrhosis counts (257 and 85, as quoted in cl_alc_cirrhosis_amount) differ. Like the frequency figures in key finding 10, this suggests the review used another analysis of the cohort, so claims should not describe the review's Danish data as 'alcoholic cirrhosis only'.

Studies and cases behind each pooled cohort category (Figure 2; editors' sums): occasional 5 cohorts and 458 cases; 1 drink 6 and 1,111; 2 drinks 6 and 574; 3-4 drinks 5 and 203; 5-6 drinks 5 and 281; 7 or more 4 and 276. Key finding 2 gives the number of sex-specific estimates (5 to 7) but not cohorts or cases.

The Results text says women's RRs were higher 'across all consumption levels' (and the abstract 'consistently higher'), but at occasional drinking the women's pooled RR (0.95) is below the men's (1.23) (Results, 3rd paragraph; Figures 3 and 4). This could be added to reporting issues; the interpretation gap covers only the Highlights' 'any alcohol consumption'.
